bullets: How place value decides what each decimal digit is worth, and how to add 0.4 + 0.25 by lining up the places
slides.heading: Decimals: place value and adding 0.4 + 0.25
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we work with decimals - tenths, hundredths, and adding 0.4 + 0.25 - and by the end you will be able to explain why 0.25 is not bigger than 0.4.

bullets: Read decimals by naming the tenths and hundredths places
Write 0.4 as 0.40 so both numbers talk in hundredths
Add decimals place by place: tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A classmate says 0.25 must be bigger than 0.4 because 25 is bigger than 4
Is that right? How big is each number really?
slides.heading: More digits, bigger number?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: 0.25 or 0.4 - which is bigger? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s4 settles this exactly.

bullets: A digit is worth its face value times its place: the 4 in 0.4 is four tenths, the 2 in 0.25 is two tenths
Tenths are bigger pieces than hundredths: ten hundredths make exactly one tenth
slides.heading: Place value decides what a digit is worth
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: where a digit stands decides what it is worth, and counting digits never decides which decimal is bigger.

bullets: Split one whole bar into ten equal parts; four shaded parts is four tenths, written 0.4
The 4 sits in the tenths place, so 0.4 means 4 out of 10 equal parts
slides.heading: Tenths: one bar, ten equal parts
slides.notes: Point at the bar as the parts shade in and narrate: each part is one tenth of the whole, and four of them make 0.4.

bullets: Split the whole square into ten rows and ten columns: one hundred tiny parts
Twenty-five tiny parts is 0.25: twenty hundredths plus five more hundredths
slides.heading: Hundredths: one square, one hundred tiny parts
slides.notes: Count the columns with the class: each column is ten hundredths, so two columns and five more tiny parts make twenty-five hundredths.

bullets: Write 0.4 as 0.40 so both numbers talk in hundredths, then line up tenths under tenths
Forty hundredths plus twenty-five hundredths is sixty-five hundredths: 0.40 + 0.25 = 0.65
slides.heading: Add: line up the places
slides.notes: Narrate the extra zero slowly: writing 0.4 as 0.40 changes nothing, and now the places line up so the addition is honest. The answer is 0.65.

bullets: Careful - the trap is: Comparing decimals by digit count: 0.25 looks bigger than 0.4 because 25 > 4.
Place value decides: 0.4 is 0.40, and forty hundredths beats twenty-five hundredths
slides.heading: Watch out: 0.25 is not bigger than 0.4
slides.notes: Contrast the two bars side by side: the tenths bar and the hundredths square cover the same whole, and 0.4 covers more of it than 0.25 does.

bullets: Work 0.4 + 0.25 in two steps: first write 0.4 = 0.40, then add the hundredths
0.40 + 0.25 = 0.65 - check each place: 4 tenths plus 2 tenths, 0 hundredths plus 5 hundredths
slides.heading: Worked example: 0.4 + 0.25
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly as in scene s3 and name each one as you write it; say: matching the place values first keeps every place honest.

bullets: Which is bigger, 0.6 or 0.45? Explain using tenths and hundredths, not digit count
Careful - a classmate says: Comparing decimals by digit count: 0.25 looks bigger than 0.4 because 25 > 4. Correct them in one sentence, naming what place value does
slides.heading: Your turn: compare, then add
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the place-value sentence first, then on the exact sentence they used to correct the claim.

bullets: On your own: work out 0.4 + 0.25, showing the 0.40 step
Watch out for the trap one last time: Comparing decimals by digit count: 0.25 looks bigger than 0.4 because 25 > 4. Say which of 0.4 and 0.25 is really bigger, and why
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the 0.40 step in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about place value in your second.
